title: OpenAI expands free ChatGPT for researchers to 200,000 with 50,000 new grants
summary: If you do research and have been on the fence about paying for ChatGPT: OpenAI is expanding free access to up to 200,000 researchers worldwide, and the next round of 50,000 grants opens November 23 on a first-come, first-served basis.
ai_summary: OpenAI is expanding ChatGPT for Academic Researchers from its small July pilot into a free program for up to 200,000 researchers worldwide. The next application round opens November 23 with 50,000 grants, first come, first served; each grant covers the recipient and up to two collaborators, so this round can reach up to 150,000 people. Two changes from the pilot: selection moves from lottery to first-come, first-served, and the free tier moves from ChatGPT Pro to Plus because OpenAI reviewed usage and said most people never hit Pro limits. By default, data shared through the program is not used to train models. It is a fit for researchers who want frontier models on their work without worrying about subscription costs; however, the regular Plus price and exact eligibility criteria are not stated in the announcement.
brief: The next round offers 50,000 free grants starting November 23, first come, first served—no lottery.
Each grant covers the recipient plus up to two collaborators, so this round can reach up to 150,000 researchers.
The free tier moves from the pilot's ChatGPT Pro to ChatGPT Plus; by default, program data is not used for training.
The pilot already had 20,000 researchers in 33 countries; respondents estimated the same work would take nearly twice as long without AI.

sections.h: What it is: OpenAI turns the pilot into a bigger free ChatGPT program for researchers

blocks.p: On November 16, 2026, OpenAI announced it is expanding its ChatGPT for Academic Researchers program. Put simply, the program gives eligible researchers free access to ChatGPT so they can use frontier models on their work without being blocked by subscription costs. It ran as a small pilot in July and is now moving into a larger round.

sections.h: How to apply: first come, first served, with each grant covering you plus two collaborators

blocks.p: Applications open Monday, November 23. The biggest change from the pilot: there is no lottery; the first 50,000 eligible applications to come in will get grants. If you're already on the waitlist and qualify, OpenAI will email you before applications open with instructions for activating your account.

fig.title: Three rule changes between the pilot and this round
fig.subtitle: Amber marks what's new this round; neutral marks the pilot approach; gray marks information the announcement doesn't give.
fig.footer: First come, first served means applying early once you're eligible is the safest path—luck no longer matters.

blocks.p: What each grant includes: the recipient plus up to two collaborators get free ChatGPT Plus. So this round's ceiling is 150,000 people—50,000 grants, with up to two collaborators each.

callout.title: 150,000 is a ceiling, not a guarantee
callout.text: The 150,000 figure is reached only if every grant includes two collaborators; the actual number depends on how many people each grant carries.

sections.h: Why switch the free tier from ChatGPT Pro to Plus?

blocks.p: The pilot offered ChatGPT Pro, the pricier tier with higher limits and more compute. After reviewing pilot usage, OpenAI says most participants would have stayed within ChatGPT Plus limits, so this round moves to Plus and uses the saved capacity to cover more teams.

callout.title: Enough for most projects, but watch heavy workloads
callout.text: If your research requires long runs of heavy computation, Plus limits may feel tighter than Pro. The announcement doesn't give specific limits for either tier, so a direct comparison isn't possible.

sections.h: Pilot results: 20,000 researchers across 33 countries, saving nearly half the time

blocks.p: Since the pilot began in July, 20,000 researchers across 33 countries have joined. OpenAI's Economic Research team published a report, Science at the Frontier: How Scientists Use ChatGPT, based on more than 1,800 pilot participants.
One striking finding: participants estimated that doing the same research at the same quality would take nearly twice as long without AI.

callout.title: How to read 'nearly twice as long'
callout.text: This is respondents' self-estimate, not a controlled experiment, so treat it with some caution.

sections.h: What researchers actually do with ChatGPT

blocks.p: The pilot surfaced two public examples: one in medicine and one in biodiversity.

fig.title: Pilot use cases: from drug targets to museum specimens
fig.subtitle: Cards are research cases mentioned in the announcement, plus one general program benefit.

items.title: Finding new drug targets
items.desc: Shuqi Li, a researcher at Brigham and Women's Hospital and Harvard Medical School, is exploring whether ChatGPT can connect lab and patient data to speed up antibiotic development—with a goal of shortening tuberculosis treatment.

items.title: Turning specimen photos into databases
items.desc: Arthur Porto's team at the Florida Museum of Natural History uses AI to turn photographs of museum specimens into searchable databases, and also built a 3D butterfly model whose wings change color as you turn it.

items.title: Frontier models + training
items.desc: Participants get access to OpenAI's frontier models and training on how to use ChatGPT in their research.

sections.h: Beyond this program: other entry points for researchers

blocks.p: ChatGPT for Academic Researchers is only one route. OpenAI also offers ChatGPT Edu for campus research, teaching, and learning, with data-analysis tools and administrative controls, and GPT-Rosalind for biology research, pairing specialized biological reasoning with scientific tools and databases.

blocks.p: The Rosalind Academic Plan gives eligible U.S. university labs up to 30 free seats for up to 12 months, but accessing GPT-Rosalind requires approval through OpenAI's trusted-access process.
In mathematics, OpenAI also contributed $5 million to a new Simons Foundation initiative to help mathematicians check, understand, and build on AI-generated results.

sections.h: Pricing and privacy: how free is it, and is data trained on?

blocks.p: On price: this round gives away ChatGPT Plus, so the 50,000 grants themselves are free. But the announcement doesn't list the regular ChatGPT Plus price or the pilot's ChatGPT Pro price, so you can't calculate exactly how much recipients save.
On privacy: by default, data shared through the program is not used to train models. Note the word 'default'—the announcement doesn't spell out exceptions.

list: The regular ChatGPT Plus price and the pilot's ChatGPT Pro price: not stated.
What exactly makes a researcher 'eligible': the announcement says only that applicants must qualify, without listing criteria.
How quickly the 50,000 grants will run out and how they'll be distributed by country: not stated.
Whether pilot researchers who got Pro will be automatically renewed or downgraded this round: not stated.
The application deadline: the announcement only says applications open November 23, not when they close.
Whether there are exceptions or opt-ins to the no-training default: not stated.

blocks.p: The value is straightforward: eligible researchers, plus up to two collaborators, get free ChatGPT Plus for their work, along with training, and by default their data isn't used for training. The trade-offs: it's only ChatGPT Plus, heavy compute may be constrained, and you have to grab a grant before they're gone.

list: If your work means constantly looking up sources, writing code, cleaning data, or drafting papers, and your team is no larger than you plus two collaborators, this round is worth applying to early.
If you're on the waitlist, check your inbox: qualifying researchers will get activation instructions before applications open.
If you're a U.S. university lab doing biology, also look at the Rosalind Academic Plan's 30 free seats.
If you need long, high-volume compute runs, confirm first that Plus limits are enough—the announcement gives no specific caps.
